title: Text taken apart and put together

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace folder. Build Dorrit's counter lines here and run them on data/counter.txt.

tasks.title: Trim a field
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/fields.cpp`, write a function called `trim` that takes a text as a reference to a `const std::string` and gives back a `std::string`: the same text without the spaces, tabs and carriage returns (`'\r'`) at its start and at its end. What is between stays as it is, and a text of only those gives back `""`.

Check calls `trim` with texts of its own: blanks at one end or both, a carriage return as a Windows line end leaves it, spaces inside, only blanks, and an empty text.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `const std::string&` in, a `std::string` back.
Find where the first character that is not blank sits.
Give back `""` when there is none.
Find the last one that is not blank, and give back the piece from the first to the last.
hints: A text can be searched from the front or from the back for the first character that is not one of a set of characters, and `.substr` from part 1 gives back a piece of it.

A search that finds nothing gives back `std::string::npos`, a position far past any end: for a text of only blanks, that is the case to answer first. The piece's length is the distance from the first to the last, plus one.

The shape is `std::size_t first = text.find_first_not_of(" \t\r"); if (first == std::string::npos) { return ""; } std::size_t last = text.find_last_not_of(" \t\r"); return text.substr(first, last - first + 1);`.

tasks.title: Split a line into fields
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function called `splitAt` that takes a line as a reference to a `const std::string` and a separator as a `char`, and gives back a `std::vector<std::string>`: the pieces of the line between the separators, in order, as they are, spaces kept. A line with 2 separators has 3 fields, an empty field counts as one, before, between or after the separators, and an empty line is one empty field. So `"3104,pocket watch,"` at `','` has 3 fields, the last one empty.

Check calls `splitAt` with lines of its own: empty fields at the start, in the middle and at the end, another separator, a line with none, and an empty line.
nextSteps: Write the first line: the line and the separator in, a `std::vector<std::string>` back.
Read the line's pieces up to each separator, and keep each one.
Look at what happens to a last field that is empty, and to an empty line.
hints: A string stream reads a text as if it were a file, and reading a line from a stream can stop at any character you name instead of the line end.
Reading pieces stops when the text ends, so a last field that is empty is never read: a line that is empty, or that ends with the separator, needs one more empty field added by hand.

The shape is `std::istringstream in(line); std::string field; while (std::getline(in, field, separator)) { fields.push_back(field); } if (line.empty() || line.back() == separator) { fields.push_back(""); }`.

tasks.title: Read a whole number, and nothing else
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `toWhole` that takes a text as a reference to a `const std::string` and gives back a `std::optional<int>`: the whole number the text holds, with spaces allowed before and after it. It gives back `std::nullopt` when the text is empty, when it does not start with a whole number, or when anything but spaces is left after the number. So `" 75 "` gives back `75`, and `"12abc"` gives back nothing.

Check calls `toWhole` with texts of its own: plain numbers, spaces around one, a number below zero, letters or a point after a number, a word, an empty text and only spaces.
nextSteps: Add the `#include` lines that `std::optional` and `std::istringstream` come from.
Write the first line: a `const std::string&` in, a `std::optional<int>` back.
Read a whole number from the text, and give back `std::nullopt` when that read fails.
Then find out whether anything other than spaces is left, and give the number back only when nothing is.
hints: Part 7 met `std::stoi`, which reads `"12abc"` as 12 and throws on `"abc"`. A string stream made from the text reads a number the way `>>` reads typing, and the stream can be asked about what follows.
After the number, try to read one more character. `>>` skips spaces first, so the read only works when something other than spaces is left: then the text is not a whole number.
The shape is `std::istringstream in(text); int number = 0; if (!(in >> number)) { return std::nullopt; } char extra = 0; if (in >> extra) { return std::nullopt; } return number;`.

tasks.title: Put a ticket line together
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `ticketLine` that takes a ticket as an `int`, an item as a reference to a `const std::string` and parts as a `double`, and gives back a `std::string`: the ticket, a comma, the item, a comma, and the parts with exactly 2 decimals, with no spaces added and no line end. For `3101`, `"mantel clock"` and `18.5`:

```
3101,mantel clock,18.50
```

Check calls `ticketLine` with tickets of its own, parts of 0 and over 1000 among them, and reads the text it gives back.
nextSteps: Write the first line: the ticket, the item and the parts in, a `std::string` back.
Make a string stream that writes into a text.
Write the three fields to it with their commas, the parts with 2 decimals.
Give back the text the stream holds.
hints: A string stream can write as well as read: everything written to it with `<<` collects in a text inside it, with all the tools `std::cout` has for numbers.
`std::to_string` of a `double` always writes six decimals. The stream writes as few as it needs, until it is told to write a set number, as part 1 did with `std::cout`.
The shape is `std::ostringstream out; out << ticket << ',' << item << ',' << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << parts; return out.str();`.
